title: Geese’s Soaring Live Show Lives Up to the Hype, With Fearless Improvisations and Boundless Energy: Concert Review

body:
There are reasons why people are so excited about Geese, the most exciting rock band to emerge from New York in decades. 

	It’s the buzz that envelops a band in the middle of an ascent, as its most recent record “Getting Killed” was passionately received by critics and fans alike. It’s the howls of excitement surrounding lead singer Cameron Winter, whose solo career lifted off at the same time as the band’s profile, to the point where the 24-year-old is getting accolades that would suffocate others. Even interviews with the band are underlined by a jittery vibe, four lifelong friends who would rather let their instruments do the talking than give a soundbite for TikTok.
	

	The Fillmore Philadelphia was pulsing in the minutes leading up to the first of the band’s two-night stand on Nov. 7. The group — Winter, guitarist Emily Green, bassist Dominic DiGesu, drummer Max Bassin and touring keyboard player Sam Revaz — set the tone for a raucous evening with set opener “Long Island City Here I Come.” With Winter percussively playing piano all the way on stage right, the track is a barreling double-time anthem for the very-loud band, punctuated by Winter belting lyrics like “I’m about to kick your ass up and down this street.” The song immediately kicked the crowd into a frenzy and felt like a clear statement of purpose: don’t confuse this for one of Winter’s solo piano shows, and if you only know the band from viral hits like “Au Pays du Cocaine” or “Taxes,” buckle up.

	The first surprise of the Geese live experience is Green’s swagger and experimentation. The guitarist is a key player in guiding the band’s more experimental moments and ferocious improvisation. Often tinkering with pedals as her fingers fly across the fretboard, she’s able to stretch a song to the outer limits, only to snap back quickly and clearly when a sharp riff is called for. Bassin also is central to the style, furiously playing all over his kit while still keeping in the pocket, ready to let loose during solos on songs such as the jumpy kiss-off “Bow Down.” DiGesu’s bass was often the steadiest instrument of the night, deep and powerful despite flights of fancy from his bandmates.
	

	Despite the uproar of the full group, Winter’s power was always evident during the band’s 80-minute set. Imposingly tall and clad in a too-tight Massive Attack T-shirt, he tinkered with lyrics and inflection on older staples like “2122” and “Cowboy Nudes,” even paying tribute to Television’s recently departed Richard Lloyd in the former. Yet some of his more impressive vocal moments came on slower songs like “Half Real,” in which he toggled both his ramshackle baritone and surprisingly delicate falsetto. Winter’s vocal range practically lifted the Fillmore into orbit during the yearning final moments of the piece.

	Despite touring the album for well over a year, with this East Coast jaunt cheekily titled the Getting Killed Again Tour, the members of Geese don’t seem to be growing tired of the material, still able to find nooks and crannies to explore and keep things fresh. The final song of the night, “Getting Killed” album opener “Trinidad,” is a fan-favorite experience of loud-quiet-loud, in which a breezy verse is interrupted the band roaring along to Winter yelling “There’s a bomb in my car!” A circle pit formed for the song, which was lengthened by the band’s bluesy interpretation, withholding energy from the crowd until they were about to burst. 

	Unsurprisingly, it made the release of the chorus that much more cathartic, a band at its peak flexing its power.

body:
Irma P. Hall, who played Josephine “Big Mama” Joseph in the 1997 dramedy “Soul Food,” died on Tuesday, her family confirmed. She was 91.

	“Irma P. Hall was a beloved actress, author, poet, educator and public speaker whose contributions touched countless lives throughout her remarkable career,” her family wrote in a statement. “Her legacy of talent, dedication and compassion will continue to inspire generations to come.”
	

	Born in Beaumont, Texas, Hall was raised in Chicago before graduating from Texas College in 1956. She became a high school teacher and taught French, Spanish and other languages in Houston and Dallas until she began acting full time in 1984.

	Her first role was as Georgia Brown in the independent film “Book of Numbers,” directed by Raymond St. Jacques. She was performing a poem when he scouted her and offered her the role on the spot. She instantly discovered her love for acting. She went on to act in several films and TV shows, including Ron Howard’s action thriller “Backdraft” in 1991 and Peter Macdonald’s comedy-drama “Mo’ Money” in 1992.

	Her career continued to grow with “Family Thing,” “Nothing to Lose” and “Steel” before she landed the role of Big Mama.

	She received the NAACP Image Award for Outstanding Supporting Actress in a Motion Picture in 1998. “Soul Food” was a hit at the box office, prompting the spinoff series “Soul Food: The Series,” where Hall reprised her role in fantasy sequences.

	In 2004, she received a Jury Prize at the Cannes Film Festival for her performance opposite Tom Hanks in “The Ladykillers.” She later made guest appearances on” Law & Order: Special Victims Unit,” “The Game” and “Chicago Fire.”

title: Russell Brand’s Pubic Hair Removed From London Museum After Rape Conviction, Curator Says ‘I Have No Desire to Hear His Name Again’
description: Russell Brand’s pubic hair is no longer on display at a London museum of curiosities following the comedian’s conviction and sentencing for rape an
body:
Russell Brand’s pubic hair is no longer on display at a London museum of curiosities following the comedian’s conviction and sentencing for rape and sexual assault.

	Viktor Wynd, the eccentric collector behind the Viktor Wynd Museum of Curiosities, Fine Art & UnNatural History in Hackney, confirmed that he removed the unusual artifact from his collection in the wake of Brand’s legal troubles.


	“I took them straight off display and have no desire to hear his name again – he has no place in my museum of horrors,” Wynd told Variety on Wednesday afternoon.
	



	

	



	The removal comes just days after Brand, 51, was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison at London’s Southwark Crown Court on Monday, Nov. 9. A jury found the former comedian and actor guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault involving four women, with the offenses taking place between 2004 and 2009, during his rise to fame in British television and Hollywood. He was acquitted of two additional rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault.

	The pubic hair had been among the more notorious items in Wynd’s collection for over a decade. According to a 2016 account of the museum, the hair was originally sent to Wynd by a woman who claimed to have shaved Brand at a Camden Town salon. The donation was accompanied by a handwritten letter explaining that she thought the collector would appreciate the unusual souvenir. The authenticity of the hair has not been independently verified.

	Opened in 2014 on Hackney’s Mare Street, Wynd’s museum is modeled after the traditional Wunderkammer, or cabinet of curiosities, and houses an eclectic assortment of macabre artifacts, natural history specimens and celebrity memorabilia. Its collection includes shrunken heads, two-headed animals, dodo bones, occult objects and a lock of Elvis Presley’s hair. The museum also houses an absinthe parlour and cocktail bar operated by the Last Tuesday Society.

title: ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ Texas Spinoff Casts ‘How to Get Away With Murder’ Alum Karla Souza in Lead Role

	The spinoff was originally announced at
body:
The “Grey’s Anatomy” spinoff set in West Texas has cast Karla Souza in a lead role, Variety has learned. 

	The spinoff was originally announced at ABC in May. It was intended to launch during the 2026-2027 broadcast season, but was recently delayed to the 2027-2028 season after it did not receive a California TV tax credit. 

	The official logline for the untitled series describes it as “an edgy drama about a team at a West Texas rural medical center — the last chance for care before miles of nowhere.”
	

	Souza will star as Dr. Carolina “Lina” Hall, who is described as “a haunted and cynical doctor who runs a medical center in a small town in West Texas.” 

	The role brings Souza back into the ABC and Shondaland fold. She previously starred in the Emmy-winning ABC series “How to Get Away With Murder” in the role of Laurel Castillo. She also starred in the ABC sitcom “Home Economics,” which aired for three seasons. Souza’s other credits include “Day Shift” at Netflix, the series “56 Days” and the film “La Caida” at Amazon, with Souza winning an International Emmy Award for the film, and the Mexican films “¿Qué culpa tiene el niño?,” “Nosotros los Nobles,” and “Instructions Not Included.” 

	She is repped by Gersh, Untitled, and Gang Tyre. 

	Shonda Rhimes and Meg Marinis are the co-creators and executive producers on the spinoff series. “Grey’s Anatomy” star Ellen Pompeo is also an executive producer, as is Betsy Beers. 20th Television and Shondaland produce. 

	This will now be the third spinoff of “Grey’s Anatomy.” In addition to the mothership show, ABC has also aired the spinoffs “Private Practice” and “Station 19,” which ran for six seasons and seven seasons respectively. ABC also aired the digital series “Grey’s Anatomy: B-Team” on ABC.com in 2018.

title: Troy Baker to Receive Legend Award at 2027 New York Game Awards (Gaming News Roundup)
description: Troy Baker has been announced by the New York Videogames Critics Circle as the recipient of the Andrew Yoon Legend Award for the 2027 New York Game
body:
Troy Baker has been announced by the New York Videogames Critics Circle as the recipient of the Andrew Yoon Legend Award for the 2027 New York Game Awards.

	With more than 400 roles across video games, television and film, Baker is one of the most well-known voice actors in the gaming industry, . He has brought to life a number of iconic video game characters, including his award-winning role as Indiana Jones for “Indiana Jones and the Great Circle.”
	

	“When we consider our upcoming Andrew Yoon Legend winners, we’re looking for individuals who’ve made a deep cultural impact on the video game landscape, and Troy Baker felt like the perfect addition,” said Harold Goldberg, NYVGCC co-founder and president. “Troy is such a force of nature within the games industry. We’ve recognized his voice-acting performances at previous New York Game Awards, and we are ecstatic to have him join our roster of Andrew Yoon Legend winners. Plus, our audiences are in for a treat with his musical performance after this year’s awards. You’ll only get to experience that moment in person at SVA Theatre!”

	Following the awards, Baker will perform a musical set on Jan. 19 at the SVA Theatre in Manhattan. All ticket holders will be able to participate in the concert as a closer to the 16th annual New York Game Awards.

	Proceeds from the Awards support NYVGCC’s Playing with Purpose writing program, which brings journalism and game narrative writing classes and workshops to New York City schools and shelters.

	See more gaming news from the week in the roundup below.
	
	
		EVENTS	

	“Star Trek” took over the Audrey Irmas Pavilion in Los Angeles Nov. 6 for the Magic: The Gathering Star Trek USS Gathering Experience.

	The multi-level immersive experience celebrated the newest Universes Beyond set, “Magic: The Gathering | Star Trek,” which launches Friday. Among the night’s attendees were “Star Trek” actors Becky Lynch, Celia Rose Gooding and Gates McFadden.

	See photos from the event below.

		MONETIZATION	

	In-game content platform Overwolf announced it paid creators over $300 million in 2025, totaling more than $800 million in total creator payouts.

	Aiming to help modders earn a sustainable living by creating games, Overwolf is targeting $1 billion in annual payouts by 2030. The company supports games including “Minecraft,” which has 240,000 mods and 93 billion downloads, and “The Sims 4,” with 100,000 mods and 2.8 billion downloads.

	Through its revenue-sharing model, creators are directly rewarded for their work. Those who opt to display ads receive a share of every dollar earned, while Premium Mod authors earn half of all revenue that is generated.
	
		TECH	

	Netflix Playground has now added full episodes of popular children’s series to its library, allowing kids to play along as they watch.

	Shows that are now available include “Doozie’s Doghouse,” “Paw Patrol,” “Peppa Pig,” “Gabby’s Dollhouse,” “Trash Trucks,” “Sesame Street,” “PJ Masks,” “Booba,” “Blippi’s Job Show,” “Red Fish Blue Fish” and “Horton.” New games were also added, including “Trash Truck,” “Sesame Street,” “Kpop Demon Hunters,” “Blippi,” “Number Blocks” and “My Very Hungry Caterpillar.”

	Included in every Netflix membership, Netflix Playground has no ads or in-app purchases. In-app shows will rotate over time.
	
		RELEASE DATES	

	In anticipation of the long awaited release of “Grand Theft Auto 6,” Xbox is making the game available through Xbox Cloud Gaming, so the game will be playable on day one.
	

	The game, which has become the most pre-ordered title of all time on the Microsoft Store, will be available on XBOX One and XBOX Series X|S, starting at 1 a.m. ET on Nov. 19.

	You can pre-order “Grand Theft Auto VI” today on the Microsoft Store.

title: FKA Twigs Becomes Josephine Baker: Inside the Lavish, Globe-Spanning Biopic from Maimouna Doucouré and Studiocanal (EXCLUSIVE)
description: On a crisp October afternoon in the Bois de Vincennes, on the outskirts of Paris, FKA twigs is transported back to 1950s America. Wearing a cream-c
body:
On a crisp October afternoon in the Bois de Vincennes, on the outskirts of Paris, FKA twigs is transported back to 1950s America. Wearing a cream-colored pinstriped coat, a dark beret and black leather gloves, the British singer and dancer has been up since the early hours, with a 4 a.m. pickup for hair and makeup to transform into Josephine Baker, the legendary entertainer and civil rights activist.

	Standing opposite her is Oscar-nominated actor Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor, who plays Baker’s mother. The two are filming a tense confrontation at a cemetery, a scene that cuts to the heart of Maïmouna Doucouré’s ambitious biopic.
	

	Between takes, FKA twigs stays in character, looking pensive and emotional. The atmosphere on set is studious and distinctly international, with cast and crew switching between English and French.

	And while the cemetery scene unfolding that afternoon is intimate, other sequences have the scale and flamboyance of a classic Hollywood production, notably those recreating the legendary Folies Bergère cabaret in Paris, where Baker became a sensation in the 1920s. The sprawling production has enlisted some 2,400 extras.

	Yet behind the lavish costumes, musical performances and sweeping historical canvas, “Josephine Baker” is ultimately a portrait of a woman whose extraordinary public life was shaped by private wounds.

	“What’s most important to me is not simply portraying Josephine as this powerful woman, this icon who was inducted into the Panthéon. We already know that side of her. I want to tell the story of the woman behind the icon,” says Doucouré, the Sundance-winning filmmaker behind “Cuties” and “Hawa,” speaking during lunch with the crew.
	

	“I want to explore her wounds, her vulnerability, her flaws, the things that shaped her and the extraordinary resilience she developed,” she says. “I think her strength becomes even more extraordinary when you understand where it comes from.”

	Rather than delivering a conventional biopic, Doucouré has built the narrative around Baker’s return to the United States in 1951, when the celebrated performer, who had found fame and freedom in France, confronted the racial segregation she had fled decades earlier. The film moves between that pivotal period and flashbacks to Baker’s childhood in St. Louis, her meteoric rise in 1920s Paris, her work with the French Resistance during World War II and her later years.

	The prestige project marks a considerable leap in scale for Doucouré and ranks among the most ambitious French-produced biopics in years. Studiocanal is co-producing with Bien ou Bien Productions, Doucouré and her partner Zangro’s banner, as well as financing and handling international sales.

	Finding the actress who could convey both Baker’s strength and vulnerability proved particularly challenging, even though FKA twigs was among the first performers Doucouré saw during the London leg of her casting search.

	Doucouré traveled from London to New York and Los Angeles, auditioning major stars and emerging performers alike. She insisted on seeing candidates perform, regardless of their fame. Each audition included singing, dancing and a demanding dramatic scene.

	“I met some incredibly talented actresses, but I couldn’t cast someone just because she was famous or even because I admired her work. I needed to see something very specific, to see Josephine come alive in front of me.”

	It happened when FKA twigs showed up. “You could tell she was nervous. You could feel how much it meant to her,” Doucouré recalls.

	“I literally started crying because suddenly I was seeing Josephine Baker. I completely forgot that I had written the scene. I forgot that I was sitting in an audition room.”

	Although she continued auditioning actresses, Doucouré couldn’t shake the impression twigs had made. “I kept thinking, ‘I found her.’”

	The British artist, whose screen credits include “Honey Boy,” “The Crow” and A24’s “Mother Mary,” had never carried a feature of this magnitude. The role demands acting, singing and dancing, with twigs portraying Baker across several decades, performing her songs and speaking French, which she didn’t previously know.
	

	“She also had to learn to speak French in a very short amount of time and master different American accents, even though she’s British,” Doucouré says. “You can’t simply switch from one accent to another. You have to show that evolution naturally.”

	Capturing Baker’s distinctive stage presence without merely imitating her was another challenge.

	“FKA twigs is an extraordinary performer, but she has her own way of moving, her own musical identity. And Josephine had such a unique physical language. The challenge wasn’t just to reproduce her movements or her voice. It was to understand what made her performances so singular and then make them feel alive rather than imitated.”

	Doucouré was determined to showcase twigs’ talents without turning the film into a conventional musical.

	“I didn’t want to make a film about Josephine Baker without showing her dancing and singing. Come on, it’s Josephine Baker! And I have FKA twigs. Of course, I’m going to make her dance and sing!”

	Bringing Baker’s life to the big screen was a formidable undertaking long before twigs came aboard. Zangro says at least 16 production companies had previously attempted it, while Baker herself had tried to develop a film about her life as far back as 1968.

	“The project had been circulating at Canal+ for more than 10 years,” he says. “At the beginning, Maïmouna and I thought we might be a little smarter than everybody else, but we very quickly realized what we’d gotten ourselves into. It was Everest.”

	The film spent four years in development, with repeated rewrites, production delays and mounting financial challenges. Baker’s extraordinary life made it difficult to determine what to include.

	“At first, I wanted to tell absolutely everything,” Doucouré says. “This woman lived 400 years!”

	“She was a pilot. She survived plane crashes. She served during World War II. She was a secret agent. She fought for civil rights. She knew Martin Luther King. She tried to save her château,” says Zangro. “When you read Josephine Baker’s biography, you almost feel like you haven’t lived your own life.”

	The breakthrough came when the filmmakers decided to anchor the narrative in one pivotal chapter rather than attempt to chronicle everything.
	

	Doucouré, who co-wrote the screenplay with Olivier Lorelle (“Days of Glory”), spent years researching Baker and working closely with her family. The project has the blessing of her sons Jean-Claude Bouillon Baker and Brian Bouillon Baker, as well as the Rainbow Tribe.

	“There are books, of course, but sometimes those books contradict one another. Who better to tell me about Josephine Baker than her own children?” Doucouré says.

	Although much of “Josephine Baker” takes place in America, the production is shooting entirely in Europe, with filming in France and Sofia, Bulgaria, through Nov. 13.

	The cast also includes Giuseppe Maggio, Grégory Montel, Benjamin Millepied, Féodor Atkine, Alex Lutz and Harmony Raine Riley.

	The movie is bound to have a broad international roll-out. Studiocanal will distribute across its own territories, including France, the U.K., Germany, Italy, Benelux, Poland, Australia and New Zealand, and is handling worldwide sales.

	“It’s not a French film made for the international market. It’s an international film in every respect, from the cast to the locations and languages,” Zangro says.

	Bringing that world to life, however, has required some creative solutions, not least because the film couldn’t afford to shoot in the United States.

	“The United States has become too expensive for filming,” Zangro says. “So we’re doing what the Americans themselves are doing. We’re going to Sofia, Bulgaria, where there are backlots where we can recreate Harlem and Broadway.”

	The filmmakers have also transformed a parking lot in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis into a street in 1918 St. Louis, complete with brick and stone buildings. Production designer Stéphane Rosenbaum, whose credits include “Moulin,” has had to conjure up everything from Roaring Twenties Paris to 1950s Miami, where a hotel suite was recreated with LED screens providing the exterior views.

	“I looked at a lot of photographs for inspiration,” Rosenbaum says. “But we’re not making a documentary, so we also had to invent a visual universe.”

	Costume designer Emmanuelle Youchnovski, whose credits include “The Substance” and “Dalida,” has been equally uncompromising.

	“We decided to make absolutely everything rather than rent costumes,” she says. “We made the hats, the shoes, even the buttons.”
	

	The production tapped artisans who work with Chanel for buttons and ornaments, commissioned embroidery from workshops in India and enlisted Faubourg 22-11, an atelier associated with Schiaparelli that worked on the famous yellow coat in “The Substance.”

	Among the biggest challenges was Baker’s iconic banana skirt, which Youchnovski had to adapt to twigs’ athletic dancer’s physique.

	“The banana skirt was a real challenge, let’s not pretend otherwise,” she says. “We made a banana skirt. We didn’t reinvent the wheel. But we approached it a little differently.”

	For Doucouré, the costume is also a reminder of Baker’s complicated relationship with the racial stereotypes of her time.

	“Of course, you can’t separate the banana skirt from the colonial stereotypes of that time. But what fascinates me is what Josephine did within those constraints. She found ways to play with those stereotypes and sometimes even turn them to her advantage. That’s where I find her so fascinating.”

	Baker was also a trendsetter who challenged prevailing beauty standards.

	“We’re talking about the colonial era, and white women were trying to look like Josephine Baker,” Doucouré says.

	Youchnovski has traced Baker’s evolution from a mischievous young performer to an international star and, later, a more modest figure, using tailored jackets and exaggerated accessories to reflect her willingness to play with masculine and feminine codes.

	“The actress absorbs the character and magnifies her. And that’s exactly what FKA twigs is doing. It’s extraordinary,” Youchnovski says.

	For Doucouré, Baker’s legacy extends far beyond entertainment. The woman who challenged segregation, fought fascism and built a multiracial family remains a powerful figure amid renewed political and racial divisions.

	Doucouré says she has debated whether Baker should be considered a feminist with one of her sons.

	“He always tells me, ‘Stop saying my mother was a feminist. Feminism didn’t exist. My mother was a humanist.’”

	“And I tell him, ‘Yes, but even if she didn’t necessarily define herself through the labels we use today, your mother challenged so many of the limits imposed on women at the time. To me, that’s deeply feminist.’”
	

	The filmmaker sees a direct connection between Baker’s struggles and the present.

	“You look back at history and think, ‘How could people have allowed these things to happen?’ And then you realize that future generations may look back at our own time and ask exactly the same question.”

	As filming draws to a close, Doucouré says she likes to imagine Baker herself watching over the production.

	“I grew up with the belief that the spirits of our ancestors watch over us. Whether that’s true or not, I don’t know. But I like to believe that Josephine’s spirit is with us.”

title: Anne Hathaway to Receive American Riviera Award at Santa Barbara International Film Festival
description: Anne Hathaway will be honored with the American Riviera Award at the 42nd annual Santa Barbara International Film Festival on Feb. 5 with an in-per
body:
Anne Hathaway will be honored with the American Riviera Award at the 42nd annual Santa Barbara International Film Festival on Feb. 5 with an in-person tribute and conversation. She will be recognized for her performance as Penelope in Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey.”

	“Anne Hathaway has always impressed me with her theatrical sophistication, unwavering commitment and remarkable versatility as a performer,” SBIFF executive director Roger Durling said in a statement. “In ‘The Odyssey,’ she delivers a breathtaking performance, one that stands among the finest of her career, channeling simmering rage and profound emotional complexity into a portrayal that is at once fierce, vulnerable, poignant and unforgettable.”
	

	The American Riviera Award was established to recognize actors who have made a significant contribution to American cinema. Previous recipients include Ethan Hawke, Zoe Saldaña, Mark Ruffalo, Brendan Fraser, Kristen Stewart, Delroy Lindo, Renee Zellweger, Viggo Mortensen, Sam Rockwell, Jeff Bridges, Michael Keaton, Rachel McAdams, Patricia Arquette, Robert Redford, Quentin Tarantino, Martin Scorsese and many more.

	In addition to “The Odyssey,” the Academy Award-, Golden Globe-, SAG- and BAFTA Award-winning actress was featured in several other films this year, including “Mother Mary,” “The Devil Wears Prada 2,” “The End of Oak Street” and “Verity,” an adaptation of Colleen Hoover’s bestselling novel. Her upcoming projects include Ron Howard’s “Alone at Dawn,” “Days of Thunder 2” with Tom Cruise and “The Princess Diaries 3,” where she will reprise her role as Mia Thermopolis.
	

	The festival will take place from Feb. 3-13. Official events include screenings, filmmaker Q&As, industry panels and celebrity tributes. Other tributes include Carrie Coon, Mariana di Girolamo, Rosalind Eleazar, Jordan Firstman, Anthony Ippolito, Jaafar Jackson and Inde Navarrette.

body:
“La Bola Negra” continues to take the world and audiences by storm. Starting next month, fans can step inside the world of the film.

	The immersive exhibition celebrating Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s film, “Love Leaves A Legacy: Creating La Bola Negra,” opens at NYA Studios East in Hollywood and is presented by Netflix and KCRW. 

	The exhibition runs from Dec. 4-6 and will celebrate Calvo and Ambrossi’s bold cinematic vision and the artistry behind the film. The works of cinematographer Gris Jordana, editor Alberto Gutiérrez, composer Raül Refree, costume designer Ana López Cobos, hair designer Pablo Morillas, makeup designer Mariló Osuna and production designer Roger Bellés will all feature.
	

	Original costumes, props, production artwork and behind-the-scenes photography exploring the film’s striking visual world will be showcased. To highlight the enduring influence of Federico García Lorca, the exhibit will also include rare books curated by the firm Peter Harrington.

	“La Bola Negra” follows Carlos González, a late-2010s historian tasked with connecting the pieces between a gay-themed Federico García Lorca play he inherits and the two other plot threads, including a narrative about the tender, illicit relationship between two soldiers on opposing sides of the Spanish Civil War (Guitarricadelafuente and Miguel Bernardeau). The queer historical drama is inspired by the unfinished final work of Spanish poet and playwright Federico García Lorca and a play by Alberto Conejero.

	Since its premiere at the Cannes Film Festival, where it received a 16-minute standing ovation and Best Director Award, “La Bola Negra” has received widespread praise. It took home the audience award at the 2026 BFI London Film Festival, Toronto International Film Festival audience prize and will receive the Gotham Vanguard Tribute award at this year’s Gotham Film Awards on Nov. 30. Guitarricadelafuente also received the Discovery Award at this year’s SCAD Savannah Film Festival. Composer Raul Refree was also honored with Variety’s 10 Artisans to Watch at this year’s SCAD Savannah Film Festival. Refree is also being honored with the composer award at this year’s Hamilton Behind the Camera Awards presented by Variety. The film will be Spain’s official submission for best international feature at the 2027 Academy Awards.
	

	Public access is available by reservation on Dec. 5 and 6. Reservations can be made via Eventbrite.
